requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in water sports activities and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that could occur while participating in water sports: blisters, cold-water shock and hypothermia, dehydration, heat-related illnesses, sunburn, sprains, strains, minor cuts and bruises, spinal injury, and concussions and head trauma. (c) Review the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy. Tell how it applies to water sports.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: A body temperature of 105 degrees or greater is a life-threatening medicalcondition and requires immediate medical treatment by health-care (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Heatstroke is a life-threatening condition; call for medical assistanceimmediately (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: While waiting for medical personnel to arrive, work to lower the victim's temperature (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Move the person to an air-conditioned or shadyarea (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Loosen tight clothing and further cool the victim by fanning and applying wet towels (p. 28).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If possible, immerse or spray the person with cold water (p. 28).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Ifyou have ice packs, wrap them in a thin barrier (such as a thin towel) and place them under the armpits and against the neck and groin (p. 28).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If the personis able to drink, give small amounts of cool water (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: BSA Swimmer Qualification Check: Swimming Ability All water-skiers and wakeboarders must have passed the Scouting America swimmer test (p. 12).
BSA Swimmer Qualification Check Principle 2: Anyone not classified as aswimmer may ride as a passenger in the boat when the operator is a skilled adult. 4 (p. 12).
BSA Swimmer Qualification Check Principle 3: Life Jackets Properly fitted U. S. Coast Guard-approved life jackets must beworn by all persons engaged in boating activity (p. 12).
BSA Swimmer Qualification Check Principle 4: Type III lifejackets are recommended for general recreational use (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (BSA Swimmer Qualification Check): Allparticipants in towed activity afloat (waterskiing, wakeboarding, kneeboarding, tubing, etc.) must wear a life jacket marked for waterskiing. 5 (p. 12).
Step 2 (BSA Swimmer Qualification Check): Buddy System All participants in water sports activities must use the buddysystem (p. 12).
Step 3 (BSA Swimmer Qualification Check): Every individual must have a buddy, and every craftshould have a buddy boat when on the water. 6 (p. 12).
Step 4 (BSA Swimmer Qualification Check): Skill Proficiency All participants in a water sports activity must be trained andexperienced in watercraft handling skills, safety (p. 12).

pamphlet_excerpts: Signals to the safety observer: The driver may use this signal to alert the skier that the boat is about to turn (p. 20).
Signals to the safety observer Principle 2: If the skier wants the driver to turn, theskier uses the same signal followed bypointing in the direction he or shewants the driver (p. 20).
Signals to the safety observer Principle 3: Once a skier is underway, the noise from the boat makes hearing instructions difficult (p. 20).
Signals to the safety observer Principle 4: The skier must learn to give directions by using the hand signals shown here (p. 20).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Signals to the safety observer): The observer serves as the eyes and the ears for the driver and skier (p. 20).
Step 2 (Signals to the safety observer): Note that "skier" refers to both water-skiers and wakeboarders (p. 20).
Step 3 (Signals to the safety observer): The observer must communicate the skier's signals to the boatdriver quickly and accurately (p. 20).
Step 4 (Signals to the safety observer): To do this, the observer mustwatch the skier closely, tell the boat driver if the skier falls, and keep the driver alert to other boat traffic (p. 20).

pamphlet_excerpts: Showing reasonable control: To keep the board from wobbling, putslightly moreweight on your front foot than onyour back foot as the boat begins Alternate Method for Deepwater (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 2: Youmay prefer to start out with the wakeboard partially rotated uptoward the front foot (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 3: Begin with the wakeboard out in front ofyou and parallel to the water's surface (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 4: Keep your knees bent and hold the rope handle with your arms straight (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Showing reasonable control): When you are in position and ready, shout out "Hit it!" to letthe driver know to accelerate (p. 59).
Step 2 (Showing reasonable control): As soon as the boat starts to pull, twist at the hips to turn the front of the board up and toward the boat (p. 59).
Step 3 (Showing reasonable control): Keeping your knees bent, transfer more weight to your back foot as the boatpulls (p. 59).
Step 4 (Showing reasonable control): Alternate starting position to pull you out of the water (p. 59).

Step 3 (While on shore): When riding a wakeboard, one foot is in front (p. 17).
